claim: GPCRs regulate all aspects of human physiology.
source: GPCRs regulate all aspects of human physiology, and biophysical studies have deepened our understanding of GPCR conformational regulation by different ligands.
evidence: This is a general statement about GPCR function that draws from established scientific consensus in the field.

claim: There is no experimental evidence for how sidechain dynamics control allosteric transitions between GPCR conformations.
source: Yet there is no experimental evidence for how sidechain dynamics control allosteric transitions between GPCR conformations.
evidence: This claim is supported by the authors' assessment of the existing literature and represents a gap in knowledge that motivates their study.

claim: Wild-type A2AR samples were generated that are deuterated apart from 1H/13C NMR probes at isoleucine δ1 methyl groups.
source: To address this deficit, we generated samples of a wild-type GPCR (A2AR) that are deuterated apart from 1H/13C NMR probes at isoleucine δ1 methyl groups, which facilitated 1H/13C methyl TROSY NMR measurements with opposing ligands.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the methods and results sections describing the labeling and expression procedures.

claim: Low [Na+] is required to allow large agonist-induced structural changes in A2AR.
source: Our data indicate that low [Na+] is required to allow large agonist-induced structural changes in A2AR, and that patterns of sidechain dynamics substantially differ between agonist (NECA) and inverse agonist (ZM241385) bound receptors, with the inverse agonist suppressing fast ps-ns timescale motions at the G protein binding site.
evidence: This claim is supported by NMR spectral data comparing A2AR in NaCl versus KCl conditions with different ligands (Figure 3).

claim: Patterns of sidechain dynamics substantially differ between agonist (NECA) and inverse agonist (ZM241385) bound receptors.
source: Our data indicate that low [Na+] is required to allow large agonist-induced structural changes in A2AR, and that patterns of sidechain dynamics substantially differ between agonist (NECA) and inverse agonist (ZM241385) bound receptors, with the inverse agonist suppressing fast ps-ns timescale motions at the G protein binding site.
evidence: This is supported by the triple quantum relaxation experiments showing different η values for different ligands (Figure 6).

claim: The inverse agonist ZM241385 suppresses fast ps-ns timescale motions at the G protein binding site.
source: Our data indicate that low [Na+] is required to allow large agonist-induced structural changes in A2AR, and that patterns of sidechain dynamics substantially differ between agonist (NECA) and inverse agonist (ZM241385) bound receptors, with the inverse agonist suppressing fast ps-ns timescale motions at the G protein binding site.
evidence: This is supported by the relaxation data showing higher η values (more rigid) for ZM241385-bound receptor compared to NECA-bound receptor.

claim: Crystals of bovine rhodopsin provided the first high-resolution picture of a GPCR's architecture.
source: Crystals of bovine rhodopsin provided the first high-resolution picture of a GPCR's architecture (Palczewski et al., 2000; Li et al., 2004), and structures of photoactivation intermediates (Nakamichi and Okada, 2006; Salom et al., 2006) and retinal-free opsin (Park et al., 2008; Scheerer et al., 2008) further documented the structural transitions involved in rhodopsin activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published crystal structures.

claim: Crystal structures of the human β2 adrenergic receptor with inverse agonists, agonists, and bound G protein provided a molecular basis for understanding how diffusible agonist binding can promote structural changes in a receptor to enhance signaling.
source: For GPCRs activated by diffusible ligands, crystal structures of the human β2 adrenergic receptor (β2AR) with inverse agonists (Rosenbaum et al., 2007; Cherezov et al., 2007), agonists (Rosenbaum et al., 2011; Rasmussen et al., 2011a; Warne et al., 2011), and bound G protein (Rasmussen et al., 2011b) provided a molecular basis for understanding how diffusible agonist binding can promote structural changes in a receptor to enhance signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published crystal structures of β2AR in different states.

claim: The overall structures of GPCRs are remarkably similar, with Cα rmsd values between unrelated receptors in the 2–3 Å range.
source: While the sequences of these GPCRs and their orthosteric ligand binding pockets are highly diverse, the overall structures are remarkably similar, with Cα rmsd values between unrelated receptors in the 2–3 Å range.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge from structural comparisons of multiple GPCR crystal structures.

claim: Common structural changes in GPCR activation include inward movements of transmembrane helices at the orthosteric pocket, rearrangements of common core residues through the helical bundle, and rigid-body outward movements of TM6 at the cytoplasmic surface.
source: For the few GPCRs that have been captured in both inactive and active conformations, common structural changes include inward movements of transmembrane (TM) helices at the orthosteric pocket, rearrangements of common core residues through the helical bundle, and rigid-body outward movements of TM6 at the cytoplasmic surface to expose G protein binding epitopes (Katritch et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a review article summarizing structural features of GPCR activation.

claim: 19F NMR and EPR experiments on the β2AR and A2AR provided evidence for at least four different conformational states populated by these receptors.
source: 19F NMR and EPR experiments on the β2AR (Liu et al., 2012a; Manglik et al., 2015) and A2AR (Ye et al., 2016) provided evidence for at least four different conformational states populated by these receptors, which are differentially stabilized by ligands of different efficacy.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published NMR and EPR studies.

claim: 1H/13C 2D NMR studies on 13Cε-methionine-labeled β2AR showed that a high free-energy barrier exists between inactive and active conformations (with exchange on the millisecond timescale).
source: 1H/13C 2D NMR studies on 13Cε-methionine-labeled β2AR (Nygaard et al., 2013; Kofuku et al., 2014) showed that a high free-energy barrier exists between inactive and active conformations (with exchange on the millisecond timescale), and agonist binding alone is only capable of weakly populating the active conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published NMR studies on β2AR.

claim: Agonist binding alone is only capable of weakly populating the active conformation of β2AR.
source: 1H/13C 2D NMR studies on 13Cε-methionine-labeled β2AR (Nygaard et al., 2013; Kofuku et al., 2014) showed that a high free-energy barrier exists between inactive and active conformations (with exchange on the millisecond timescale), and agonist binding alone is only capable of weakly populating the active conformation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published NMR studies on β2AR.

claim: Ligand-activated GPCRs are weakly coupled allosteric systems in which multiple energetic inputs (i.e. agonist and G protein binding) are required to predominantly populate the active conformation.
source: These studies, in addition to similar measurements on μ-opioid receptor chemically modified to introduce NMR-active 13C-methyl labels onto lysine residues (Sounier et al., 2015), suggest that ligand-activated GPCRs are weakly coupled allosteric systems in which multiple energetic inputs (i.e. agonist and G protein binding) are required to predominantly populate the active conformation.
evidence: This claim is an inference drawn from multiple cited NMR studies on different GPCRs.

claim: The importance of repacking of sidechains from TM3, TM5, and TM6 beneath the ligand binding pocket, known as the 'conserved core triad,' was identified by comparison of structures of β2AR and the μ-opioid receptor.
source: The importance of repacking of sidechains from TM3, TM5, and TM6 beneath the ligand binding pocket, known as the 'conserved core triad,' was identified by comparison of structures of β2AR (Rosenbaum et al., 2011; Rasmussen et al., 2011a) and the μ-opioid receptor (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to crystal structures of β2AR and μ-opioid receptor.

claim: An activated microswitch near the site of G protein binding represents a common feature of GPCRs that have been crystallized in both active and inactive conformations.
source: Further down the TM bundle, an activated microswitch near the site of G protein binding has been found to represent a common feature of GPCRs that have been crystallized in both active and inactive conformations (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published analysis of GPCR structures.

claim: Perdeuteration and ILV labeling conventionally rely on expression in E. coli.
source: A major hurdle in carrying out such experiments is that perdeuteration and ILV labeling conventionally rely on expression in E. coli (Goto et al., 1999), while wild-type GPCRs typically require a eukaryotic host to ensure proper folding, glycosylation, trafficking, and stability in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a published method for ILV labeling in E. coli.

claim: Wild-type GPCRs typically require a eukaryotic host to ensure proper folding, glycosylation, trafficking, and stability in the plasma membrane.
source: A major hurdle in carrying out such experiments is that perdeuteration and ILV labeling conventionally rely on expression in E. coli (Goto et al., 1999), while wild-type GPCRs typically require a eukaryotic host to ensure proper folding, glycosylation, trafficking, and stability in the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about GPCR expression requirements.

claim: The authors generated highly-deuterated 1H/13C Ile δ1-methyl labeled proteins in Pichia pastoris.
source: We have addressed many of these practical issues with our generation (Clark et al., 2015) of highly-deuterated 1H/13C Ile δ1-methyl labeled proteins in Pichia pastoris, a methylotrophic yeast (Cereghino and Cregg, 2000) that is adaptable to D2O-based minimal media, will utilize the Ile precursor α-ketobutyrate, and enables expression of GPCRs at levels sufficient for crystallography (Shimamura et al., 2011; Hino et al., 2012; Yurugi-Kobayashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the authors' previous work and is demonstrated in the current manuscript.

claim: A2AR is an important regulator of vascular function.
source: Here we apply this labeling method to the wild-type human A2AR, an important regulator of vascular function with a well-developed pharmacology including the natural hormone adenosine and high-affinity synthetic agonists and antagonists (Preti et al., 2015; de Lera Ruiz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles on A2AR pharmacology.

claim: A2AR has been crystallized in inactive, intermediate and active conformations.
source: A2AR has been crystallized in inactive (Jaakola et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012b), intermediate (Lebon et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011) and active (Carpenter et al., 2016) conformations, and has been studied by 19F NMR to characterize its conformational equilibria (Ye et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple crystal structures of A2AR.

claim: The authors expressed and purified milligram quantities of labeled wild-type human A2AR.
source: We expressed and purified milligram quantities of labeled wild-type human A2AR and were able to resolve 20 out of 29 expected peaks in the Ile δ1 region in 1H/13C TROSY HMQC experiments.
evidence: This is supported by the methods and results sections describing the purification protocol and yields.

claim: 20 out of 29 expected peaks in the Ile δ1 region were resolved in 1H/13C TROSY HMQC experiments.
source: We expressed and purified milligram quantities of labeled wild-type human A2AR and were able to resolve 20 out of 29 expected peaks in the Ile δ1 region in 1H/13C TROSY HMQC experiments.
evidence: This is directly supported by the NMR spectra shown in Figure 2.

claim: Four signals were assigned to specific functionally important residues through structure-guided mutagenesis, including I923.40 of the conserved core triad and I292 at the cytoplasmic surface.
source: Through structure-guided mutagenesis, we assigned four of these signals to specific functionally important residues, including I923.40 of the conserved core triad (Huang et al., 2015) and I292 at the cytoplasmic surface.
evidence: This is supported by the mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Kd for [3H]-ZM241385 binding to A2AR was 0.42 nM in NaCl-containing buffer.
source: The Kd for [3H]-ZM241385 was 0.42 nM in NaCl-containing buffer, while the Ki for NECA was 210 nM in low ionic strength and 420 nM in KCl-containing buffer, in agreement with previous binding studies (Xu et al., 2011; Carpenter et al., 2016; Bertheleme et al., 2013) on heterologously expressed A2AR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the radioligand binding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The Ki for NECA was 210 nM in low ionic strength and 420 nM in KCl-containing buffer.
source: The Kd for [3H]-ZM241385 was 0.42 nM in NaCl-containing buffer, while the Ki for NECA was 210 nM in low ionic strength and 420 nM in KCl-containing buffer, in agreement with previous binding studies (Xu et al., 2011; Carpenter et al., 2016; Bertheleme et al., 2013) on heterologously expressed A2AR (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by the radioligand binding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Saturating the receptor with the full agonist NECA led to an 8-fold stimulation of [35S]GTPγS binding.
source: Saturating the receptor with the full agonist NECA led to an 8-fold stimulation of [35S]GTPγS binding, and the inverse agonist ZM241385 produced a 50% reduction in basal activity, similar to values measured for protonated A2AR (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the GTPγS binding data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The inverse agonist ZM241385 produced a 50% reduction in basal activity in [35S]GTPγS binding assays.
source: Saturating the receptor with the full agonist NECA led to an 8-fold stimulation of [35S]GTPγS binding, and the inverse agonist ZM241385 produced a 50% reduction in basal activity, similar to values measured for protonated A2AR (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the GTPγS binding data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The perdeuterated A2AR is capable of activating Gs at wild-type levels in vitro.
source: These data show that the perdeuterated A2AR is capable of activating Gs at wild-type levels in vitro, and can serve as a valid model for GPCR dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the GTPγS binding data comparing protonated and deuterated A2AR.

claim: The chemical shifts of the agonist-bound and inverse agonist-bound A2AR are similar in the presence of 150 mM NaCl.
source: Overall, in a liganded sample, we could resolve 20 peaks in the Ile δ1 region of the spectrum, out of 29 Ile residues present in our construct (28 from the receptor and one from the C-terminal Protein C tag). The chemical shifts of the agonist-bound and inverse agonist-bound A2AR are similar (Figure 2A,B), showing subtle changes that are comparable in magnitude to those observed previously for 13C-methyl-methionine probes in β2AR (Kofuku et al., 2014; Kofuku et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the NMR spectra in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: The spectrum of the unliganded (apo) A2AR shows a loss of most of the well-dispersed peaks present in the ligand-bound spectra.
source: The spectrum of the unliganded (apo) A2AR shows a loss of most of the well-dispersed peaks present in the ligand-bound spectra (Figure 2C), which could result from protein instability or conformational exchange on the μs-ms timescale.
evidence: This is directly observed in the NMR spectrum shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The spectrum of NECA-bound A2AR is dramatically different in KCl compared to NaCl.
source: The spectrum of NECA-bound A2AR, on the other hand, is dramatically different in KCl and NaCl (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), with multiple peaks shifting and decreasing in intensity.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the NMR spectra in Figure 3B and 3D.

claim: The spectrum of ZM241385-bound receptor in KCl is very similar to that in the presence of NaCl.
source: The spectrum of ZM241385-bound receptor in KCl is very similar to that in the presence of NaCl (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), with the peak assigned to I923.40 shifting slightly upfield in the 13C dimension.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the NMR spectra in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: The average peak intensity in the Gd3+-DTPA containing spectrum is about 0.4 of that in the control spectrum.
source: Examining our data, we see that the average peak intensity in the Gd3+-DTPA containing spectrum is about 0.4 of that in the control spectrum, suggesting that the Ile δ1 methyl groups of A2AR in the DDM micelle are quite close to solvent on average (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by the solvent PRE data shown in Figure 4.

claim: I2747.39 is solvent-exposed due to its presence in the solvent-exposed ligand-binding pocket.
source: The accessibility of I2747.39 is expected due this amino acid's presence in the solvent-exposed ligand-binding pocket.
evidence: This is an inference based on the crystal structure and the solvent PRE data.

claim: I2386.40 is in close proximity to the Na+ site in ZM241385-bound A2AR.
source: In ZM241385-bound A2AR, this residue is also in close proximity to the Na+ site (Liu et al., 2012b), one packing layer toward the cytoplasmic surface.
evidence: This is based on the crystal structure of ZM241385-bound A2AR.

claim: Pairing five allowed spectra with a single forbidden spectrum at 8 ms relaxation delay can faithfully recapitulate the η values measured using five pairs of forbidden and allowed experiments.
source: We found that pairing five allowed spectra with a single forbidden spectrum, we were able to faithfully recapitulate the η values measured using five pairs of forbidden and allowed experiments (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of η values from different experimental setups shown in Figure 5.

claim: The average η value for the ZM241385-bound sample is higher than for NECA, indicative of greater overall rigidity of sidechains with inverse agonist.
source: The average η value for the ZM241385-bound sample is higher than for NECA, indicative of greater overall rigidity of sidechains with inverse agonist.
evidence: This is supported by the relaxation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: I292 shows the largest difference between ligands, becoming more flexible in the NECA-bound sample.
source: Among the other assigned peaks, I292 shows the largest difference between ligands, becoming more flexible in the NECA-bound sample.
evidence: This is supported by the relaxation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: I923.40 and I2747.39 display more modest increases in flexibility with agonist.
source: I923.40 and I2747.39 display more modest increases in flexibility with agonist, while the dynamics of I2386.40 are largely unchanged by ligand (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the relaxation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The dynamics of I2386.40 are largely unchanged by ligand.
source: I923.40 and I2747.39 display more modest increases in flexibility with agonist, while the dynamics of I2386.40 are largely unchanged by ligand (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by the relaxation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The differences in fast timescale dynamics occur in the presence of NaCl, in which chemical shifts for the agonist- and inverse agonist-bound states were nearly identical.
source: Interestingly, these differences in fast timescale dynamics occur in the presence of NaCl, in which chemical shifts for the agonist- and inverse agonist-bound states were nearly identical.
evidence: This is an observation that integrates the chemical shift data (Figure 2) with the dynamics data (Figure 6).

claim: The S2axis order parameters for some methyl groups show significant variations across different windows in MD simulations, suggesting that slower timescale motions involving these residues contribute to the sidechain dynamics measured on the fast timescale.
source: The S2axis order parameters for some methyl groups (for example, I60 and I80 in ZM241385; I106 and I302 in NECA) show significant variations across different windows, suggesting that slower timescale motions involving these residues contribute to the sidechain dynamics measured on the fast timescale.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the MD simulation data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The differences between ZM241385- and NECA-bound dynamics at three of the four assigned sites (I2386.40, I2747.39, and I292) from MD simulations are qualitatively similar to what is observed by NMR.
source: Interestingly, the differences between ZM241385- and NECA-bound dynamics at three of the four assigned sites (I2386.40, I2747.39, and I292) are qualitatively similar to what we see by NMR.
evidence: This is a comparison between the MD simulation data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and the NMR data (Figure 6).

claim: The Na+ site first seen in the high-resolution structure of A2AR bound to ZM241285 is conserved throughout most Class A GPCRs.
source: The Na+ site first seen in the high-resolution structure of A2AR bound to ZM241285 is conserved throughout most Class A GPCRs, and Na+ exerts a negative allosteric effect on A2AR activation by bridging residues on TM3 and TM7 and stabilizing the inactive conformation (Liu et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: Na+ exerts a negative allosteric effect on A2AR activation by bridging residues on TM3 and TM7 and stabilizing the inactive conformation.
source: The Na+ site first seen in the high-resolution structure of A2AR bound to ZM241285 is conserved throughout most Class A GPCRs, and Na+ exerts a negative allosteric effect on A2AR activation by bridging residues on TM3 and TM7 and stabilizing the inactive conformation (Liu et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the crystal structure and functional studies.

claim: A 9-fold decrease in NECA affinity is observed when A2AR membranes are incubated in 150 mM NaCl buffer versus 150 mM KCl buffer.
source: For A2AR expressed in P. pastoris, we observe a 9-fold decrease in NECA affinity when membranes are incubated in 150 mM NaCl buffer versus 150 mM KCl buffer (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), similar to previously reported values (Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the binding data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: I2747.39 at the ligand binding site makes direct contact with the adenine or adenine analogue rings of both NECA and ZM241385 in their respective crystal structures.
source: I2747.39 at the ligand binding site makes direct contact with the adenine or adenine analogue rings of both NECA and ZM241385 in their respective crystal structures (Jaakola et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012b; Lebon et al., 2011; Carpenter et al., 2016) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is based on analysis of crystal structures.

claim: I2747.39 was more rigid in terms of its fast sidechain motions with inverse agonist bound, and more flexible with NECA occupying the binding pocket.
source: In our relaxation datasets, I2747.39 was more rigid in terms of its fast sidechain motions with inverse agonist bound, and more flexible with NECA occupying the binding pocket.
evidence: This is supported by the relaxation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: MD simulations on β2AR predicted greater mobility of agonists relative to inverse agonists in the orthosteric pocket of the inactive-state structure.
source: In addition, MD simulations on β2AR predicted greater mobility of agonists relative to inverse agonists in the orthosteric pocket of the inactive-state structure (i.e. not bound to Gs) (Dror et al., 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published MD simulations.

claim: The fast dynamics of residues at the orthosteric pockets of Class A GPCRs may be correlated with the functional efficacy of the bound ligand.
source: Our data suggests that the fast dynamics of residues at the orthosteric pockets of Class A GPCRs may be correlated with the functional efficacy of the bound ligand.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the authors' data and previous studies.

claim: I923.40 is one of the three residues of the conserved core triad in A2AR, along with P1895.50 and F2426.44.
source: The residue I923.40 is one of the three residues of the conserved core triad in A2AR, along with P1895.50 and F2426.44, which interact at a layer beneath the orthosteric pocket further toward the cytoplasmic surface (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and established knowledge about the conserved core triad.

claim: A lower η value for I923.40 in the NECA dataset versus ZM241385 indicates greater sidechain flexibility when A2AR is agonist-bound.
source: Consistent with the rearrangements of this microswitch region between the inactive and active conformations of multiple GPCRs, we observe a lower η value for I923.40 in the NECA dataset versus ZM241385, indicating greater sidechain flexibility when A2AR is agonist-bound.
evidence: This is supported by the relaxation data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Crystal structures of A2AR bound to agonists alone showed an intermediate active-like conformation in the region surrounding I923.40.
source: In contrast, crystal structures of A2AR bound to agonists alone (Figure 7B) showed an intermediate active-like conformation in the region surrounding I923.40 (Lebon et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to crystal structures.

claim: Agonist alone (even with high [Na+]) is enough to promote the fast motions of the sidechains in the I923.40 microswitch region.
source: However agonist alone (even with high [Na+]) is enough to at least promote the fast motions of the sidechains in this microswitch, which may reduce the activation energy for the observed packing rearrangement to the active conformation.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dynamics data in the presence of NaCl.

claim: I2386.40 is one helical turn on TM6 above L2356.37, which participates in a conserved microswitch between inactive and active conformations for multiple GPCRs.
source: I2386.40 is situated further toward the G protein binding site at a critical region for GPCR activation, where it packs against TM7 and undergoes significant outward movement in the transition to the active conformation (Figure 7C). I2386.40 is also one helical turn on TM6 above L2356.37, which participates in a conserved microswitch between inactive and active conformations for multiple GPCRs (Venkatakrishnan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a published analysis of GPCR structures.

claim: I292 is present at the linker between TM7 and Helix 8, where it packs against Y2887.53 of the highly conserved NPXXY motif.
source: I292 is present at the linker between TM7 and Helix 8, where it packs against Y2887.53 of the highly conserved NPXXY motif (Katritch et al., 2013) (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and is supported by a citation.

claim: In the structure of A2AR/mini-Gs, the engineered Gs protein makes direct contact with I292 at the TM7-Helix 8 junction.
source: Further, in the structure of A2AR/mini-Gs (Carpenter et al., 2016), the engineered Gs protein makes direct contact with I292 at the TM7-Helix 8 junction.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the crystal structure.

claim: The inverse agonist activity of ZM241385 could partly arise from its allosteric suppression of dynamics at the cytoplasmic end of TM7.
source: Our data suggest that the responsiveness of sidechain dynamics to ligands in these two regions may be largely uncoupled, and that the inverse agonist activity of ZM241385 could partly arise from its allosteric suppression of dynamics at the cytoplasmic end of TM7.
evidence: This is a speculative inference drawn from the dynamics data.

claim: Modifications to the MFα signal sequence greatly increased the amount of fully-processed receptor present at the plasma membrane.
source: Modifications to the MFα greatly increased the amount of fully-processed receptor present at the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by the Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Approximately 0.5 mg of monodisperse biochemically pure wild-type A2AR in DDM detergent can be purified from 1 L of Pichia culture.
source: We developed a purification protocol for A2AR from Pichia-derived membranes, in which we can solubilize and purify ~0.5 mg of monodisperse biochemically pure wild-type A2AR in dodecylmaltoside (DDM) detergent from 1 L of culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the purification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The perdeuterated purified A2AR reconstituted with Gs heterotrimer shows an 8-fold stimulation of [35S]GTPγS binding with saturating NECA.
source: Saturating the receptor with the full agonist NECA led to an 8-fold stimulation of [35S]GTPγS binding, and the inverse agonist ZM241385 produced a 50% reduction in basal activity, similar to values measured for protonated A2AR (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the functional assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The peak for I923.40 appears to shift and simultaneously drop in intensity in the A2AR-Gs complex spectrum.
source: In the A2AR-Gs complex spectrum (Figure 2D), the peak for I923.40 appears to shift and simultaneously drop in intensity, strongly suggesting that I923.40 is involved in conformational changes on several timescales while the receptor is bound to Gs.
evidence: This is an observation from the NMR spectrum shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The environment surrounding I2386.40 is loosely packed in A2AR structures, with an ordered solvent network that may allow for relative freedom of motion for this sidechain.
source: As mentioned above, the environment surrounding I2386.40 is loosely packed in A2AR structures, with an ordered solvent network that may allow for relative freedom of motion for this sidechain.
evidence: This is an inference based on structural analysis and the dynamics data.

claim: Outward movement of TM6 is one of the hallmarks of GPCR activation seen in crystal structures.
source: Outward movement of TM6 is one of the hallmarks of GPCR activation seen in crystal structures, and the cytoplasmic ends of TM6 and TM7 are separated from each other in the structures of β2AR and A2AR bound to Gs (Rasmussen et al., 2011b; Carpenter et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from crystal structures and is supported by citations.
